description.text: Despite being lacking a brain, heart, or lungs, it possesses hundreds of tiny, glowing blue dots on its shell that act as sensitive light receptors.

description.text: Mantis shrimp strike with club or spear arms so fast they create cavitation bubbles—tiny shockwave “explosions” that stun prey.

description.text: Cleaner shrimp set up “stations,” waving long white antennae to invite fish clients. They pluck parasites and dead skin  earning protection for their service.

description.text: Their bright patterns warn of potent chemical defenses. Some steal stinging cells from their prey and reuse them as toxic armor.

before.description: Deep-sea sea cucumbers feed on organic particles on or near the seafloor. Their soft bodies and feeding tentacles come in many shapes across species.

description.text: Deep-sea cucumbers look remarkably soft, blobby, and fleshy—often resembling a cross between a worm and a gelatinous slug.

before.description: Brittle stars move with slender, flexible arms joined to a central disc. Many can shed an arm to escape a predator and later regrow it.

description.text: Brittlestars  have five long, snakelike arms that easily snap off and regrow to help them escape predators.

description.text: Often described as a resilient underwater tank, this living fossil features a tough exoskeleton. It can survive years between feedings.

description.text: Often described as a resilient underwater tank, this living fossil features a tough exoskeleton. It can survive years between feedings.

before.description: Giant tube worms live at hydrothermal vents. Without a mouth or gut, adults rely on internal bacteria that use chemicals from vent fluids to make food.

description.text: Lives in pitch-black, toxic environments relying on symbiotic bacteria for food. It builds a tough, protective tube to bear harsh temperatures.

before.description: Peacock squid have large eyes and nearly transparent bodies. Light organs beneath the eyes help hide their silhouettes from predators below.

description.text: It emits faint bioluminescent light from photophores located just beneath its eyes to help camouflage it’s silhouette.

before.description: Atolla jellyfish can flash rings of blue bioluminescence when disturbed. This burglar-alarm display may draw larger predators toward an attacker.

description.text: It possess the unique ability to flash bioluminescent blue when attacked to attract other predators to scare off the attacker.

before.description: To hunt they hover right above the seafloor and "hoover" up worms, snails, and crustaceans, swallowing their prey whole.

description.text: To hunt they hover right above the seafloor and "hoover" up worms, snails, and crustaceans, swallowing their prey whole.

before.description: A Portuguese man o' war is a colony of specialized zooids. Its gas-filled float rides at the surface while long, stinging tentacles capture prey below.

description.text: Despite looking like a single animal, the Portuguese man o' war is actually a bizarre colony of thousands of genetically identical, clones called zooids.

before.description: Blue sea dragons float upside down at the surface. They eat animals such as the Portuguese man o' war and store stolen stinging cells for defense.

description.text: It survives by eating highly venomous creatures like the Portuguese Man O' War, stealing their stinging cells, to use for it’s own defense.

before.description: Market squid live only about six to nine months. They gather to mate and lay egg capsules on the seafloor, then die after spawning.

description.text: After mating in massive swarms, the entire population dies within a year, leaving their fertilized eggs to hatch the next generation.

before.description: The Australian box jellyfish has a cube-shaped bell and clusters of eyes. Its long tentacles carry powerful venom for catching fish and shrimp.

description.text: Considered the most venomous marine creature on Earth, it carries a potent venom that can kill a human within just two to five minutes of a sting.

before.description: Parrotfish scrape food from reef surfaces with beak-like teeth, helping produce sand. Some species sleep inside protective mucus cocoons.

description.text: They scrape algae with a beak-like bite, grinding coral into fine sand. Some wrap in a nighttime mucus cocoon to hide their scent from predators.

before.description: Protected by a rigid, box-like body, longhorn cowfish graze on small bottom-dwelling prey. When severely stressed, they can release toxic mucus.

description.text: When severely threatened, the longhorn cowfish secretes a potent neurotoxin creating an invisible cloud that can kill any creatures in close proximity.

before.description: Frogfish hide among reef growth and lure prey with a modified dorsal-fin spine. Their expanding mouths suck in unsuspecting animals in a rapid gulp.

description.text: Frogfish vanish in plain sight. They “fish” with a built-in lure, then gulp prey with one of the fastest strikes in the ocean.

before.description: Often called a "rattail" because of its slender, whip-like tail, this deep-sea fish can live for over 70 years in extreme pressures.

description.text: Often called a "rattail" because of its slender, whip-like tail, this deep-sea fish can live for over 70 years in extreme pressures.

before.description: Female humpback anglerfish carry a lure lit by symbiotic bacteria. It dangles above the mouth, drawing prey close in the darkness of the deep sea.

description.text: The tip of their dorsal fin contains a glowing sac of bioluminescent bacteria used to attract prey in the pitch-black ocean depths.

before.description: A transparent dome protects the barreleye's tubular green eyes. The eyes can rotate from looking upward to facing forward as the fish feeds.

description.text: The barreleye boasts a cockpit-like, see-through head that allows its internal organs and green eyes to be visible.

holo.name: Barrel Eye Fish
holo.description: A transparent dome protects the barreleye's tubular green eyes. The eyes can rotate from looking upward to facing forward as the fish feeds.

description.text: The barreleye boasts a cockpit-like, see-through head that allows its internal organs and green eyes to be visible.

before.description: Fangtooth fish have enormous teeth for their small bodies. Special sockets in the roof of the mouth make room for the long lower fangs.

description.text: A small but fearsome-looking deep-sea predator renowned for having the largest teeth-to-body ratio of any fish in the ocean.

before.description: The black swallower has an elastic stomach that can hold prey larger than itself. This adaptation helps it take advantage of scarce deep-sea meals.

description.text: A deep-sea fish known for its highly distensible stomach, allowing it to consume prey over twice its length and 10 times its mass.

before.description: Tripod fish stand above the seabed on three elongated fin rays. Facing into the current, they spread their pectoral fins to help detect drifting prey.

description.text: Completely blind, it rests on the ocean floor using three extraordinarily long, stiff fin rays to both elevate its body and move prey to it’s mouth.

before.description: Halfbeaks have a long lower jaw and a much shorter upper jaw. These surface-dwelling fish may leap or skip across the water to escape predators.

description.text: Many halfbeak species are capable of breaching the water's surface to "fly" or skip across the waves to escape predators, much like flying fish.

before.description: Needlefish hunt near the surface with long jaws lined with sharp teeth. When startled, they can leap clear of the water.

description.text: Needlefish are hyper-fast, slender ocean hunters known to skip across the water at speeds up to 40 mph, sometimes running into swimmers.

before.description: Krill are small, shrimp-like crustaceans that gather in dense swarms. These shifting groups provide food for whales, seals, seabirds, and fish.

description.text: A highly concentrated, massive defensive swarm of krill containing up to millions of individual crustaceans.
